text:
It is reported that the land is managed for wildlife by the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission pursuant to an agreement with the Crescent Land and Timber Company (Application and Supplemental Enclosure No. 4).
The Bearcamp Creek Reservoir would remove about 520 acres from use as wildlife habitat and eliminate hunting and most wildlife in that area. Staff would expect that impacts on wildlife species due to the impoundment and construction and clearing activities at the Bearcamp Creek site would be similar in type to but greater in quantity than those described in Subsection 3.1.2 for the Bad Creek site.
Bearcamp Creek, classified as rainbow trout water by the State of North Carolina, supports some fishing for both rainbow and brook trout (Fish, 1968). About 2.2 miles of Bearcamp Creek and its tributaries would be impounded by the Bearcamp Creek Reservoir. Any fish species and other fauna dependent on a stream environment would be lost unless they could adapt to reservoir conditions.
Approximately 0.5 miles of Bearcamp Creek between the dam and Lake Jocassee, and portions of the lake would experience an increase in turbidity due to construction of the project. Turbidity would subside as disturbed areas are regrassed or reforested. Increased turbidities in portions of Bearcamp Creek and Lake Jocassee could adversely affect populations of benthic organisms and fish species utilizing such organisms as a food source. It is unknown how long it would take for such adverse effects on fish and other aquatic organisms to diminish in Bearcamp Creek and Lake Jocassee. Stream flow of Bearcamp Creek could be reduced below the upper reservoir, further affecting the suitability of the stream for fish production, especially for trout. The trout fishery could also be adversely affected if waters differing in quality were used to augment flow in Bearcamp Creek below the dam.
8.3.2.3 Water Quality
Although water quality data are not available for this stream, Staff expects that the water is of high quality, similar to that of other tributaries to Lake Jocassee. Construction of this proposed project would adversely affect about 0.5 mile of Bearcamp Creek between the dam and Lake Jocassee, and portions of the lake itself. Continual releases from the upper reservoir would be required in order to maintain flow in Bearcamp Creek during operation.
